title: Authority in Capernaum (Mark 1:21–28)
hookLine: in the synagogue he teaches with authority, and an unclean spirit shrieks
tomorrow: a mother-in-law and a whole town

cards: Saturday morning in Capernaum, a fishing town on the north shore of the lake. It's the Sabbath, and the town is at the synagogue. A visiting teacher is invited to speak, which was normal.
How he speaks isn't. People lean in. Then, in the middle of it, a scream.
A man with what Mark calls an unclean spirit is shrieking at the teacher, as if something inside him knows exactly who this is and is terrified. Everyone freezes.

teach.b: Mark says, in the King James Bible: "And they were astonished at his doctrine: for he taught them as one that had authority, and not as the scribes."

The scribes were careful teachers, and good ones often taught by citing earlier teachers: this rabbi said, that sage said. The Greek for authority is exousia, from a verb meaning it is allowed, it's in your power.
So exousia is the right to act, and to say so. Jesus speaks as if the right is his own, with no footnote. Mark never says what he taught that morning, just how it landed.
Then the scream: "Let us alone; what have we to do with thee, thou Jesus of Nazareth? art thou come to destroy us? I know thee who thou art, the Holy One of God."
The odd thing: in Mark, the spirits are the first to recognize who Jesus is, before the disciples, before the crowds.
And Jesus doesn't want their announcement: "Hold thy peace, and come out of him." Gentle in English; the Greek is blunt: be muzzled. Be quiet.

teach.h: HOLD THY PEACE, AND COME OUT OF HIM.
teach.b: Then: come out. The man convulses, the spirit cries out, and it's gone. And the town talks about one thing: what is this?
A new teaching, with authority, and even the unclean spirits obey him. Christians read these stories in different ways. Many understand them as real encounters with spiritual evil.
Many also hear in them every voice that holds a person captive and won't let go. Either way, the authority that teaches also frees. One word, and the man got his life back.

how: Many Christians read Mark's healing and deliverance stories as signs of Jesus's authority over evil; churches differ in how they understand unclean spirits today, and many pray for freedom from whatever binds a person.

authority: the right to act and to say so
great physical strength or force of will

games.q: you're teaching in the synagogue. a man shrieks: I know who you are, the Holy One of God! what do you do?
o: thank him for saying who you are.
tell the spirit to be quiet and come out.
games.why: "hold thy peace, and come out of him." the spirit is silenced, the man is freed, and the town asks: what is this?

practice: Many people carry a voice inside that doesn't help, the one that says you're not enough, you'll fail, nobody wants you here; listen for it gently, without arguing, and notice what it says and how old it sounds.
If the voice is heavy or frightening, that's something to share with someone you trust or a professional, not to carry alone.
If you pray, bring it to God with the story's words, be quiet, come out; if you don't, simply set it down.

wordCard.voice: Exousia, the right to act and to say so: spoken as his own, it teaches, and it frees.

orig.note: Greek: authority, the right or power to act, from exestin, it is allowed.

carryVoice: Your line: be quiet, come out. A voice that tears you down doesn't get to run the room. See you tomorrow.
